title: China Trade Data Gap, Arctic Route, FMC Action
metaDescription: ImportGenius finds $100bn gap in US-China trade data. China completes first Arctic container season. FMC threatens COSCO with $16.7m penalty.
bottomLine: A $100 billion gap between what China reports shipping to the US and what US Customs records receiving points to transshipment, mis-invoicing or both. The Arctic route carried 14,000 TEU this summer with half the transit time of Suez, dominated by high-value cargo. COSCO faces a potential $16.7 million penalty for ignoring an FMC order for 223 days.

stories.headline: $100bn gap between China export figures and US import data
stories.tldr: ImportGenius found a $100 billion difference between China's reported exports to the US and US recorded imports in 2025, suggesting transshipment or value manipulation.
stories.whatHappened:
ImportGenius normalised shipment-level bill-of-lading data into TEUs and cross-referenced container counts against US Census dollar values to derive value per container. Comparing that metric to China's TEU-normalised figures produced a discrepancy the company described as major and mystifying.

Michael Kanko of ImportGenius said possible explanations include transshipment through third countries such as Vietnam, incorrectly recorded shipment values, and tariff optimisation. The platform's users are increasingly using shipment records to vet customers for sanctions compliance, including confirming whether an aviation parts buyer in Turkey had transacted with Russia within the past 30 days.
stories.whyItMatters:
If a substantial portion of China-origin goods are being routed through Vietnam or other countries to avoid tariffs, you are competing with sellers who undercut your landed cost by mis-declaring origin. That pricing pressure is real whether you follow the rules or not.

The data gap also means macro trade figures are unreliable for forecasting lane capacity or rate movements. Carriers and freight forwarders base capacity decisions on Census data, but if $100 billion of volume is missing or misattributed, published utilisation rates are wrong.

If Customs tightens enforcement on transshipment or origin verification, expect longer clearance times and more documentary requests. Goods that moved quickly under a Vietnam or Malaysia certificate of origin will start getting held. Budget extra days and have your factory paperwork in order before the container leaves Asia.
stories.hotTake: The gap is large enough that someone is either lying at scale or Customs is not checking. Either way, the current system rewards whoever is willing to play games with the paperwork. That works until it stops working, and when enforcement tightens it will hit the compliant and non-compliant equally because Customs does not sort by intent when they start pulling containers.
actions: Request certificates of origin and commercial invoices from your factory before shipment and verify the stated origin matches where production actually occurred
Add two days to your US customs clearance assumption for goods transshipped through third countries or claiming non-China origin
Run your Turkey or other non-China supplier names through ImportGenius or a similar platform to check their recent shipment history for red flags

stories.headline: China finishes first scheduled Arctic container season with 14,000 TEU
stories.tldr: Sea Legend Shipping completed eight westbound Arctic voyages from China to Europe carrying 14,000 TEU, with transit times half that of the Suez route.
stories.whatHappened:
Sea Legend Shipping launched weekly container service from Ningbo-Zhoushan and other Chinese ports to Europe via the Northern Sea Route in August, deploying up to seven low or moderate ice-class container ships. The company completed the majority of planned sailings but ended departures earlier than scheduled after forecasts indicated Arctic sea ice would expand in October. The final two vessels departed Ningbo on 27 September.

The season carried more than 14,000 TEU of export cargo across eight voyages. Ningbo Customs reported that cargo through its jurisdiction totalled 7,761 TEU worth 5.33 billion yuan ($750 million), dominated by energy-storage equipment, power batteries and new-energy vehicles. The Arctic route takes about 18 to 20 days between China and Northern Europe, roughly half the transit time of traditional routes via Suez.
stories.whyItMatters:
Eighteen to twenty days from China to Northern Europe changes your Q4 restocking math if you are shipping high-value goods where a week matters. The route carried energy storage, batteries and electric vehicles, all categories where unit value justifies a premium and speed reduces working capital tied up in transit.

The seasonal window is narrow. Departures stopped in late September, meaning you have no Arctic option from October through July. If you plan to use this route, you book in summer or you wait a year. That limits it to sellers with predictable demand curves and enough volume to commit months in advance.

The cargo mix tells you who is already using it: sellers of goods worth enough per TEU that a 50% transit reduction pays for itself. If your average container value is below $100,000 and you are shipping to the UK or Western Europe, the Suez route or even air freight to a lower-tier gateway will beat the Arctic on total cost.
stories.hotTake: The Arctic route is a tool, not a revolution. It works for a narrow band of sellers shipping specific goods to specific markets during a three-month window. Everyone else will read about it and do nothing, which is the correct response.
actions: Request Arctic routing quotes from your forwarder for any Q2 2027 shipments to Northern Europe with container values above $150,000
Compare the Arctic premium to air freight from secondary Chinese gateways like Hangzhou or Nanjing for the same lane and transit window
Add Sea Legend and NewNew Shipping to your forwarder RFQ list if you regularly ship batteries, energy storage or EVs to Europe

stories.headline: FMC threatens COSCO with $16.7m penalty for ignoring payment order
stories.tldr: COSCO delayed payment of a $24,328 FMC reparations award for 223 days, prompting a show cause order with potential penalties up to $16.7 million.
stories.whatHappened:
The Federal Maritime Commission filed a show cause order against COSCO for delaying payment of a demurrage and detention award. The FMC ordered COSCO to pay Agribusiness Holdings $24,328.80 in reparations plus interest by 20 January 2026 after finding that COSCO had failed to properly issue invoices for D&D fees. COSCO did not pay for 223 days despite repeated contacts.

Under current statutes, the FMC can impose inflation-adjusted penalties of $14,988 per day, with each day considered a separate violation. If the violation is found to be wilful and knowing, the penalty jumps to $74,943 per day. COSCO's 223-day delay could result in civil penalties between $3.345 million and $16.725 million. The FMC emphasised that disregard of binding orders can undermine its authority.
stories.whyItMatters:
If the FMC follows through and hits COSCO with a penalty in the millions for ignoring a $24,000 order, it signals that the Commission is willing to use the nuclear option to enforce compliance. That changes the risk calculation for carriers who have been treating FMC orders as optional.

For you, this matters because D&D disputes are common and the power imbalance is real. Carriers issue invoices, you dispute them, the process drags, and the carrier often collects or withholds equipment regardless of merit. If the FMC starts imposing penalties large enough to matter, carriers will have to take shipper complaints seriously earlier in the process.

The flip side is that this also raises the stakes for frivolous disputes. If the FMC is willing to penalise carriers for ignoring orders, they will also expect shippers to comply with rulings that go the other way.
stories.hotTake: COSCO ignored a $24,000 order for seven months, which suggests they either do not care or they assumed the FMC would not act. The FMC is now deciding whether to prove them wrong in a way that gets noticed.
actions: Review any outstanding D&D disputes with COSCO or other carriers and escalate unresolved cases to the FMC if you have documentation that invoices were issued improperly
Keep contemporaneous records of all demurrage and detention invoices, including timestamps, amounts and the specific charges, in case you need to file a complaint
Add a line to your forwarder SOP requiring them to flag any D&D invoice that arrives more than 30 days after container return, as late invoicing is a common FMC violation

stories.headline: US commits China to 10 million tonnes of coal annually in 2027-28
stories.tldr: China agreed to import at least 10 million tonnes of US coal in each of 2027 and 2028, following a similar commitment on soybeans.
stories.whatHappened:
On 25 September the White House announced that China would import at least 10 million tonnes of US coal in each of 2027 and 2028. On 28 September China's Ministry of Commerce included coal in its reciprocal tariff-reduction framework. The commitment covers US supply overall but does not allocate the volume by loading coast, coal grade or vessel size.

Recorded sailings show 918,364 tonnes of coal shipped from the US Gulf to China in January-September 2026, against 51,726 tonnes a year earlier. August and September alone accounted for 695,375 tonnes, close to 76% of the 2026 total. The recovery nonetheless remains below the 2024 level: China took 4.6% of US Gulf coal exports this year against 9.8% in 2024.
stories.whyItMatters:
Coal and soybean commitments are part of managed trade, where volumes and lanes get allocated by governments rather than markets. That distorts container and bulk capacity in ways that affect your rates even if you never ship a tonne of either commodity.

If 10 million tonnes of coal loads from the US Gulf to China in 2027, that pulls bulk tonnage into the Atlantic that would otherwise be available for other routes. Bulk and container markets are separate, but port congestion, bunker demand and backhaul economics overlap. More US-China bulk volume means tighter vessel supply on backhaul lanes and potentially higher bunker costs that carriers pass through as fuel surcharges.

The commitment also signals that US-China trade is being managed at the commodity level rather than liberalised. If your product category becomes part of a similar commitment structure, your factory price or your shipping lane could change overnight based on a number agreed in a government office.
stories.hotTake: Managed trade commitments are bad for everyone except the companies that win the allocations. They create artificial demand, distort pricing and add political risk to commercial decisions.
actions: Monitor US-China commodity commitments in your product category or adjacent categories, as these can change tariff treatment or quotas with minimal notice
Factor potential backhaul rate increases into your Q2 2027 ocean freight budget if you ship from China to the US East Coast or Gulf
Ask your forwarder whether they expect US Gulf port congestion to increase in 2027 due to higher bulk volumes, and adjust your transit time assumptions accordingly

faq.question: Why is there a $100 billion gap between China and US trade data?
faq.answer: ImportGenius found a $100 billion difference between what China reported shipping to the US and what US Customs recorded in 2025. Possible causes include transshipment through third countries like Vietnam to avoid tariffs, mis-declared shipment values, and tariff optimisation. The gap suggests large-scale mis-reporting or that Customs is not verifying claims. This means aggregate trade data is unreliable for forecasting capacity and indicates that enforcement on origin verification may tighten, leading to longer clearance times.

faq.question: How long does the Arctic shipping route from China to Europe take?
faq.answer: The Arctic Northern Sea Route takes 18 to 20 days from China to Northern Europe, roughly half the Suez Canal transit time. Sea Legend Shipping completed eight voyages in summer 2026, carrying 14,000 TEU of high-value cargo including batteries and electric vehicles. The route operates only during summer, with departures ending in late September due to ice. Service resumes next summer. The route works for high-value containers where speed reduces working capital costs, but seasonal limits restrict broader use.

faq.question: What happens if a carrier ignores an FMC payment order?
faq.answer: The FMC can impose civil penalties of $14,988 per day for violations, or $74,943 per day if wilful and knowing. COSCO delayed payment of a $24,328 award for 223 days, resulting in potential penalties between $3.3 million and $16.7 million. The FMC stated that disregard of orders undermines its authority. For shippers, this signals more aggressive enforcement, raising stakes for both carriers and shippers in demurrage, detention and invoice disputes.

faq.question: How does the US-China coal commitment affect container shipping rates?
faq.answer: China committed to import at least 10 million tonnes of US coal annually in 2027-28. This pulls bulk vessel capacity into the Atlantic, tightening supply on backhaul lanes and increasing bunker costs that carriers pass through as surcharges. Whilst bulk and container markets are separate, port congestion, bunker demand and backhaul economics overlap. More US Gulf to China bulk volume can mean higher backhaul rates and possible port congestion affecting transit times.

faq.question: Should I use the Arctic route for shipping from China to Europe?
faq.answer: The Arctic route works only for high-value goods during summer months when the speed premium justifies cost. The route carried containers averaging over $96,000 per TEU in 2026, dominated by batteries and energy storage. Transit time is 18-20 days, half that of Suez. Departures run August to late September only. If your container value is below $100,000, stick with traditional routes. Request quotes in spring for summer departures if your cargo fits.
